explanations.explanation: They say, “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God…” (Ezra 4:2). That's a hand held out, asking to join the work. I think it sounds friendly, but the next verses show how Zerubbabel, governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), answers it. Hold onto your oven mitts.

explanations.answer: To pay for the cedar logs
explanations.explanation: No money gets offered here, friend. These folks ask to join the work itself: “Let us build with you…” (Ezra 4:2). Nobody pulls out a wallet and nobody mentions lumber. Their ask is to be on the crew.

Guard duty never comes up. The enemies of Judah and Benjamin walk up to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), and ask for a spot on the building crew. Their words are “Let us build with you…” (Ezra 4:2). Standing watch with a spear isn't in this verse.

I can see why you'd lean that way, since they say they seek the same God. But the answer is no. Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the family heads reply, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God…” (Ezra 4:3). There's no handshake and no welcome here.

That's right, they turn the offer down flat. The text says, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the other family heads say it together. It's a short answer, with no hedging.

Cyrus king of Persia is the one. Zerubbabel and the family heads say they must build “as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). They point to the king's command as the reason. Their answer rests on that command.

Esar-haddon, king of Assyria, does show up in this passage, so I get the mix-up. He's the king the enemies say brought them to the land (Ezra 4:2). But he isn't the one who commanded the building. Zerubbabel and the family heads name Cyrus king of Persia (Ezra 4:3).

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is the one who came and besieged Jerusalem (Daniel 1:1). He doesn't give the building command in this passage. Zerubbabel and the family heads say, “as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). That's a different king with a different job.

The text says the people of the land “set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.” (Ezra 4:4). They don't start with swords here. They start with fear and discouragement. That can wear a builder down.

explanations.answer: Tax them for using the land
explanations.explanation: Taxes come up later in this chapter, but not in this verse, and not from these folks as a charge on the land. Here the people of the land “set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.” (Ezra 4:4). Their goal is to scare the builders. Nobody sends a bill.

Nobody gets shipped anywhere in this verse. The people of the land try to “discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.” (Ezra 4:4). The aim is to shake the builders up so they quit. They want the work to stop, and they don't move anybody out.

Darius king of Persia is the answer. The counselors work against Judah “throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” (Ezra 4:5). That's a long stretch of kings, and the frustrating never lets up.

Belshazzar is a king from Daniel's book (Daniel 5:1), but he isn't in this verse. The text names two Persian kings here. The counselors keep going “down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” (Ezra 4:5).

Sennacherib was king of Assyria and attacked the fortified cities of Judah (2 Kings 18:13). He's from a different story. In Ezra 4:5, the counselors work from the reign of Cyrus “down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” Both are Persian kings.

Aramaic it is. The letter “was written in Aramaic and then translated.” (Ezra 4:7). Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their associates wrote it to King Artaxerxes. I wrote my first recipe in a language only I could read, so I respect the translation step.

The text doesn't say Hebrew, friend. It says the letter “was written in Aramaic and then translated.” (Ezra 4:7). The letter came from Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their associates, and it went to King Artaxerxes. The text names the language plainly.

Greek isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The letter to King Artaxerxes “was written in Aramaic and then translated.” (Ezra 4:7). Bishlam, Mithredath and Tabeel sent it. Aramaic is the language the text gives.
Rehum and Shimshai call Jerusalem “that rebellious and wicked city.” (Ezra 4:12). That's their description in the letter to the king. I'm only retelling what they wrote, and those are their words.
Great is a nice word, but it's not the one they chose. Rehum and Shimshai write of “that rebellious and wicked city.” (Ezra 4:12). Nobody in that letter is handing out compliments.
Distant doesn't show up in the letter. Rehum and Shimshai call Jerusalem “that rebellious and wicked city.” (Ezra 4:12). They're describing the city's character, not how far away it is.

The letter says if the city is rebuilt, “they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” (Ezra 4:13). Tribute, duty and toll are payments that go to the king. Rehum and Shimshai are talking about his money. If I wanted a king's attention in a hurry, I'd mention the treasury too.

Rent is never mentioned in this letter. Rehum and Shimshai warn the king that “they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” (Ezra 4:13). Those payments belong to the king. The warning is about his treasury.

No wages come up. The letter says if the city is rebuilt, “they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” (Ezra 4:13). Rehum and Shimshai are pointing at what the king stands to lose. His treasury is the worry in the letter.

They tell him “that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). They say he'll find in those books that the city is a rebellious city. Rehum and Shimshai hand the king a way to check their claim. That's confident, I'll give them that.

Nobody suggests asking the priests, friend. Rehum and Shimshai say “that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). The proof they point to is written down in the king's own records. The city's own people never get asked.

The letter never points the king to anything from Cyrus. Rehum and Shimshai say “that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). They send the king to the old records. Cyrus's command (Ezra 4:3) doesn't come up in their letter.

The letter warns that “you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Dominion means the king's rule over that whole region. Rehum and Shimshai end on the biggest worry they can think of. It's like closing an email with "URGENT" in capital letters.

Allies sounds close, but it isn't the word. The letter says the king “will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Dominion means rule over the region. Rehum and Shimshai are warning about losing his rule.

Trade isn't in this warning. Rehum and Shimshai write, “you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Their last line is about the king's rule over the whole region. It's the heaviest thing they could put in a letter to a king.

explanations.answer: It revolted against kings long ago
explanations.explanation: The king says, “It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition.” (Ezra 4:19). He issued a decree and the search turned this up. That's what Artaxerxes reports back. It's his own search result.

explanations.answer: It had never been ruled by kings
explanations.explanation: The search found the opposite. The king says the city “has revolted against kings from ancient times…” (Ezra 4:19). He even says that “mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem…” (Ezra 4:20). Kings ruling there is exactly what the text tells us.

explanations.answer: It had always lived in peace
explanations.explanation: Peace isn't what the search turned up, friend. The king says, “It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition.” (Ezra 4:19). That's his report of what the search found. Quiet it was not.

It's true. The king says, “And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them.” (Ezra 4:20). He's pointing at Jerusalem's past under those kings. He remembers the payments, too.

The text says otherwise, friend. King Artaxerxes states, “And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them.” (Ezra 4:20). So he does say it, tribute and all.
Stop is the word. The king says, “Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). That's a halt order, and it goes to Rehum and Shimshai. Work stops.
Hurry would be the opposite of what he says, friend. The king tells them, “…issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). He wants the work halted. Nobody gets a faster pace.
Leaving isn't in the order. The king says, “…issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). The word is stop, which means the work halts. The text doesn't say the men have to go anywhere.
The king does leave a door cracked, though. His order says the city “will not be rebuilt until I so order.” (Ezra 4:21). That word “until” matters. Nowhere does he say never.
That's right. The king says the city “will not be rebuilt until I so order.” (Ezra 4:21). He says "until," not "never." It's a pause with a condition attached.

explanations.answer: Go to Jerusalem and stop the work by force
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. When the king's letter was read to them, “they went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them.” (Ezra 4:23). Rehum, Shimshai and their associates move right away. I think that's a hard moment, and the next verse shows the work ceasing (Ezra 4:24).

explanations.answer: Wait a whole year and then send word
explanations.explanation: Nobody waits around. Once the letter is read, Rehum, Shimshai and their associates “went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them.” (Ezra 4:23). The word is immediately. That's a hard moment to read.

explanations.answer: Write the king back asking for details
explanations.explanation: No follow-up letter shows up here. Once the king's letter is read, they “went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them.” (Ezra 4:23). Immediately means the very next thing they do is go. The text mentions no questions and no waiting.
